$comment: RAGE exposure-db (AWS) — every place customer-controlled credentials/secrets can leak, per service. Each site maps to the RAGE edge it emits (`emits`), the FULL collection recipe (`read`: access_mode/operation/params/response_path/encoding + required_permissions), where it sits (location/location_kind), and what leaks (data_kinds). Vocabulary in exposure-db/vocabulary.json.

sites.description: Access Analyzer findings expose external principals, resource ARNs, policy conditions, CloudTrail access identities, and account relationships; they do not include secret key material.
Archive-rule filter values are customer-controlled strings and can reveal sensitive principal or resource identifiers.
Access Analyzer resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
The root-account primary email is sensitive recovery data.
Account contact information contains names, addresses, and phone numbers used for account administration and recovery.
Billing, operations, and security alternate contacts expose names, emails, titles, and phone numbers.
ExportCertificate returns an exportable certificate's private key encrypted only by the caller-supplied passphrase.
An imported certificate's unencrypted PEM private key is supplied as a write-only API request field.
Certificate identity fields can disclose internal hostnames, user identities, or private infrastructure naming.
ACM certificate tag values are plaintext metadata.
Issued certificates and chains can disclose internal identities, DNS names, account structure, and certificate extensions.
A CA signing request can expose private PKI subject names and requested identity attributes, though not the private key.
Private CA tag values are plaintext metadata.
Amplify app environment variables are returned as plaintext configuration.
Branch-specific environment overrides are plaintext and may expose deployment credentials.
Amplify buildspec YAML contains commands and can hard-code credentials.
The Amplify webhook URL contains an unguessable token that can trigger builds and must be treated as a secret.
Amplify build logs can echo environment variables, package tokens, and command output; GetJob returns a pre-signed log URL.
Amplify app tag values are plaintext metadata.
API Gateway returns API-key values when IncludeValue is explicitly requested.
REST API stage variables are plaintext maps and are commonly misused for credentials or backend connection strings.
Integration URIs, request parameters, and VTL templates can hard-code backend credentials or sensitive constants.
HTTP/WebSocket API stage variables are plaintext customer values.

sites.location: CloudWatch Logs API Gateway execution/access log event.message
sites.description: Execution logging with data tracing or permissive access-log formats can capture request/response headers, bodies, authorizer context, and query tokens.
API Gateway tag values are plaintext metadata.
AppFlow connector profiles store database, OAuth, API-key, and SaaS credentials supplied through write-only credential structures.
Flow connector and task property maps can contain query literals, object paths, filter values, and sensitive transformation parameters.

read.response_path: destination records selected by flow tasks

sites.description: AppFlow copies full source records to destinations such as S3, Redshift, Snowflake, and SaaS systems; sensitive fields can be exposed at the destination.
AppFlow flow and connector tag values are plaintext metadata.
Customer-authored HTTP header match values can accidentally contain bearer tokens, API keys, or confidential routing values.
App Mesh resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
App Runner code and image services expose plaintext runtime environment maps through DescribeService.
Build and start command strings can contain inline command-line credentials.
App Runner resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Athena SQL text is retained and can contain literal credentials or sensitive predicates.
Athena result rows expose arbitrary data selected from S3, Glue, and federated sources.
Saved named-query SQL can persist sensitive literals indefinitely.
Prepared statement definitions are plaintext SQL and can include embedded sensitive constants.
Athena notebook cells and outputs can contain hard-coded credentials, queries, and sampled sensitive data.
Athena workgroup and data-catalog tag values are plaintext metadata.
Legacy launch configurations retain base64-encoded EC2 user data containing bootstrap secrets.
Lifecycle-hook notification metadata is arbitrary plaintext delivered to the hook target and may contain credentials.
Auto Scaling group tag values propagate to instances and are readable in group configuration.
Service-specific restore metadata is a plaintext string map and can retain sensitive configuration copied from the protected resource.

sites.location: StartRestoreJob recovery point -> restored resource data
sites.description: A recovery point can contain every secret present in the protected resource; AWS Backup has no generic content-read API, so inspection requires restoration into the source service.
Backup-vault policy JSON can contain customer-supplied condition values and identifiers.
Backup resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Batch job definitions can persist plaintext environment variables across ECS, Fargate, and EKS job backends.
Job parameters, commands, and arguments are customer-controlled plaintext and are often used to pass credentials.
Resolved per-job parameters and environment values may retain plaintext credentials on the submitted job record.
Batch resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Elastic Beanstalk environment properties are plaintext option values and are frequently misused for credentials.
Saved configuration templates retain option values, including environment variables and third-party settings.
Application bundles and .ebextensions/platform hooks can contain hard-coded credentials and configuration files.
Elastic Beanstalk environment and application-version tag values are plaintext.

sites.location: bedrock-runtime InvokeModel/Converse request body and response body
sites.description: Model prompts, tool inputs, retrieved context, and responses can contain credentials or confidential data; runtime responses are not retained by a generic read API unless logging is enabled.

sites.location: Configured S3/CloudWatch Bedrock model invocation log record
sites.description: Model invocation logging can persist full request and response data, including prompts and completions, in S3 or CloudWatch Logs.
Prompt Management templates and examples are customer-authored text and can contain copied credentials or confidential context.
Agent instructions and prompt overrides are persisted customer text and can expose sensitive operational data.
Inline API schemas and function definitions may contain example secrets, backend URLs, or confidential business logic.
Bedrock model-customization, agent, knowledge-base, and prompt tag values are plaintext metadata.
Parameters without effective NoEcho protection are returned by DescribeStacks and frequently contain deployment credentials.
Stack outputs are always plaintext; NoEcho does not redact values copied into Outputs.

sites.location: GetTemplate.TemplateBody (Parameters.Default, Metadata, Mappings, Resources properties, Outputs)
sites.description: CloudFormation templates can hard-code credentials anywhere; NoEcho only masks parameter display and does not protect Metadata, mappings, resource properties, or outputs.
Provider errors and custom-resource responses can echo sensitive resource properties into stack event status reasons.
CloudFormation stack tag values are plaintext and propagate to supported resources.
CloudFront origin custom headers are returned in distribution configuration and are often used as shared origin-authentication secrets.
CloudFront Function JavaScript source can contain hard-coded credentials or tokens.
CloudFront KeyValueStore values are application-controlled strings and can be misused as a secret store.

sites.location: S3 CloudFront standard or real-time log record
sites.description: CloudFront logs can contain URI query strings, cookies, headers selected for real-time logs, and client identifiers.
CloudFront distribution and function tag values are plaintext metadata.

sites.location: CloudHSM client PKCS#11/JCE/OpenSSL key object with EXTRACTABLE=true

read.response_path: protocol key bytes or wrapped key bytes

sites.description: An HSM user can export key material that was created or imported as extractable; access is governed by CloudHSM user credentials, not an AWS read API.

sites.location: CloudHSM CLI user create/change-password password input

read.operation: CloudHSM CLI user create / user change-password

sites.description: CloudHSM user passwords are supplied to the cluster client and can leak through shell history or automation even though they are not AWS control-plane fields.
CloudHSM cluster tag values are plaintext metadata.
CloudTrail preserves service request and response fields as JSON; services redact known secret fields, but arbitrary parameters, tags, URLs, and custom payloads can still leak sensitive data.
CloudTrail Lake query results expose selected event fields across event data stores.
CloudTrail Lake SQL can contain literal values used in investigations; query text is submitted in plaintext and appears in query metadata.
CloudTrail trail and event-data-store tag values are plaintext metadata.
CloudWatch Logs event messages are arbitrary application and service output and are one of the broadest plaintext credential exposure surfaces in AWS.
Logs Insights results can return any parsed field from selected log events, including credentials and PII.
Recent Logs Insights query text can persist sensitive literals pasted into filters or parse expressions.
Dashboard JSON, especially custom widgets and URLs, can contain tokens, endpoints, or sensitive query parameters.
Alarm descriptions are free-form plaintext and can contain incident data or pasted credentials.
Custom metric dimension values are plaintext and may accidentally encode usernames, account identifiers, or tokens.
CloudWatch Logs resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Package assets can contain source, binaries, configuration, package-manager tokens, and credentials.
CodeArtifact returns a bearer authorization token usable by package managers against permitted repositories.
CodeArtifact domain and repository tag values are plaintext metadata.
CodeBuild PLAINTEXT environment variables are returned directly by BatchGetProjects.
Inline buildspec YAML and command strings can contain hard-coded credentials.
Per-build environment overrides are retained on build records and may contain one-time plaintext secrets.
Builds can export environment values into CodePipeline; exporting secrets makes them visible in build metadata and downstream actions.

read.response_path: log event message or object body

sites.description: Build commands can echo environment values, credential files, package tokens, and command arguments into durable logs.
When returned for a provider webhook, the webhook secret is sensitive signing material.
CodeBuild project tag values are plaintext metadata.
Repository files and historical blobs can contain hard-coded secrets, including values deleted from the current branch.
Commit messages are durable plaintext and may accidentally include credentials or incident data.
Code review comments are user-controlled plaintext and can expose pasted tokens or debugging data.
CodeCommit repository tag values are plaintext metadata.
An inline AppSpec document can contain hook commands or configuration values with embedded credentials.

read.operation: GetDeployment then s3:GetObject or repository read

sites.description: Deployment revision bundles can include scripts, configuration files, and hard-coded secrets.

sites.location: Target host or Lambda deployment CloudWatch Logs event.message
sites.description: Lifecycle hook scripts and deployment agents can echo credentials into host files or CloudWatch logs.
CodeDeploy application and deployment-group tag values are plaintext metadata.
Action configuration maps can contain OAuth tokens, deployment parameters, command fragments, or third-party credentials; some provider secrets are redacted but arbitrary values are not.
Pipeline variable defaults are plaintext and should not be used for secrets.
Action output variables are retained in execution metadata and can expose values emitted by build or deployment actions.
Third-party and custom actions can write arbitrary execution summaries that may echo credentials or command output.
CodePipeline tag values are plaintext metadata.
A Cognito user-pool app client configured to generate a secret exposes that client secret through DescribeUserPoolClient.
Standard and custom user attributes are readable plaintext and applications may misuse them to store secrets.
Cognito Sync dataset records contain application-defined user data and can hold plaintext credentials.
Cognito user-pool tag values are customer-controlled plaintext.
AWS Config stores serialized resource configuration and supplementary data; upstream services redact known passwords, but arbitrary metadata, user data, policies, and custom fields may remain.
Advanced-query results return selected fields from stored resource configurations across an account or organization.
Aggregator advanced-query results return selected configuration fields across linked accounts and Regions.
Config rule input parameters are plaintext JSON and custom rules may use them for tokens, endpoints, or sensitive thresholds.
Automatic-remediation parameters are plaintext and can pass static credentials or sensitive values into SSM Automation.
AWS Config resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
The landing-zone manifest is customer-controlled JSON and can carry account emails, identifiers, or accidental secrets.
Enabled-control parameter values are arbitrary documents and can include misplaced sensitive values.
Control Tower resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Data Pipeline object fields can store database passwords, command arguments, shell scripts, and connection strings as plaintext.
Pipeline parameter values are plaintext and often feed credential-bearing object fields.
Task runners receive resolved pipeline objects and credentials; the polled task map can expose every plaintext field needed by an activity.
Data Pipeline tag values are plaintext metadata.
Detective's behavior graph aggregates IAM principal, access-key ID, IP, Kubernetes, process, and service activity; it does not normally retain secret key values.
Detective graph tag values are plaintext metadata.
A Direct Connect virtual interface's BGP authentication key is returned in the virtual-interface description.
Generated router configuration can include BGP authentication material and detailed network configuration.
Direct Connect resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
DocumentDB collections contain arbitrary BSON documents and can store plaintext credentials or sensitive data.
DocumentDB master passwords are write-only plaintext API inputs.

sites.location: CloudWatch Logs event.message for DocumentDB profiler/audit logs
sites.description: Profiler and audit logs may record command text, namespaces, user names, and application-supplied query values.
DocumentDB cluster parameter values are plaintext strings.
DocumentDB resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Directory administrator and reset passwords are supplied in plaintext request fields and are never returned by DescribeDirectories.
The service-account password used by AD Connector is supplied to ConnectDirectory and is not returned by read APIs.
The inter-forest trust password is a plaintext write-only API input.
Directory tag values are plaintext and may include identity or credential material.
DynamoDB item attributes are arbitrary application data and may store plaintext credentials.
DynamoDB Streams retain old and new item images, which can expose deleted or rotated secrets.
A table resource policy can contain customer-authored sensitive condition values.
DynamoDB table tag values are plaintext metadata.
EBS Direct APIs expose raw snapshot blocks that may contain files, deleted data, credentials, and private keys.
Snapshot descriptions are free-form plaintext and can contain misplaced credentials or internal identifiers.
Snapshot tag values are plaintext metadata.
Instance user data commonly contains bootstrap scripts and may expose embedded passwords, API keys, or cloud credentials.
Every launch-template version can retain base64-encoded user data containing long-lived secrets.
Boot and console output can echo user-data commands, configuration files, tokens, and application secrets.
EC2 returns a newly generated private key only in the CreateKeyPair response.
Windows administrator password data is returned encrypted to the instance key pair and becomes plaintext after private-key decryption.
EC2 resource tag values are plaintext and broadly enumerable.
OCI/Docker image manifests and embedded labels or annotations can contain sensitive build metadata or credentials.
Container image layers preserve files from every build layer and commonly expose deleted .env files, package credentials, and private keys.
Repository policy JSON is customer-authored and can contain sensitive condition values.
ECR repository tag values are plaintext metadata.
Plaintext container environment values in task definitions are readable by anyone with DescribeTaskDefinition.
Container commands and health-check command strings may embed command-line credentials.
Log-driver option maps are plaintext and some third-party drivers accept endpoints or authentication values.
Docker label maps are customer-controlled plaintext and may contain build metadata, endpoints, or misplaced credentials.
RunTask and StartTask overrides can place one-off plaintext secrets in environment values or commands retained on the task description.
ECS resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
EFS stores arbitrary files; plaintext credentials are readable through NFS when network, IAM, and POSIX controls permit.
EFS resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Kubernetes Secret objects hold base64-encoded credential material and are readable through the cluster API when EKS access and Kubernetes RBAC allow it.
Pod, Deployment, Job, and DaemonSet specifications can contain plaintext environment values and command-line credentials.
ConfigMaps are not secret stores but are frequently misused for plaintext credentials and application configuration.
EKS add-on configuration is stored as a JSON string and can contain arbitrary customer-supplied values.
EKS cluster tag values are plaintext metadata.

sites.location: Redis GET/MGET/SCAN or Memcached get response value
sites.description: Cache entries are arbitrary application values and frequently contain sessions, tokens, and credentials; normal cache authentication is outside AWS control-plane IAM.
The Redis AUTH token is supplied as a write-only API request field and is not returned by describe operations.
ElastiCache user passwords are write-only plaintext request values.
ElastiCache tag values are plaintext metadata.
An ALB OIDC action stores a client secret supplied in a write-only request field; DescribeListeners does not return it.
ALB fixed-response bodies are customer-controlled plaintext and can accidentally publish secrets to clients.
Redirect host, path, and query templates can embed tokens or send sensitive values to another endpoint.

sites.location: S3 ELB/ALB/NLB access log object body
sites.description: Load-balancer access logs can retain request paths, query strings, user agents, and client identity data; query parameters may include credentials.
Load balancer and target group tag values are plaintext metadata.
EMR configuration classifications are arbitrary property maps and can contain database, metastore, or application credentials.
Bootstrap action arguments are retained plaintext and can pass secrets to initialization scripts.
EMR step arguments and properties can contain plaintext credentials passed to Spark, Hadoop, or custom JARs.
EMR Serverless Spark/Hive parameters and configuration overrides can retain plaintext credentials.

sites.location: S3 or CloudWatch EMR step/bootstrap/application log
sites.description: EMR logs can expose full command lines, configuration values, sampled records, and application errors.
EMR resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Custom EventBridge event detail is arbitrary JSON and is copied to targets, archives, and logs; it is not directly readable from the event bus.
Rule targets can persist static JSON, headers, query parameters, and templates containing credentials.
Event-pattern constants are stored in plaintext and may reproduce real account identifiers, tokens, or sensitive payload fragments.
EventBridge Connection credentials are supplied through write-only authorization fields; DescribeConnection intentionally omits the secret values.
EventBridge Scheduler target input is persisted plaintext JSON and delivered on every invocation.
Event bus, rule, archive, connection, and scheduler tag values are plaintext metadata.
Firewall Manager managed-service data is service-specific customer-authored JSON and can contain WAF custom values, third-party settings, or accidental secrets.
Policy resource-tag selectors are plaintext and can expose sensitive classification values.
Firewall Manager policy and resource-set tag values are plaintext metadata.

sites.location: Mounted FSx file or object bytes (SMB/NFS/Lustre/ONTAP/OpenZFS)
sites.description: FSx file systems hold arbitrary customer files; content reads use the file-system protocol and identity model rather than a universal AWS API permission.
FSx for Windows accepts the self-managed AD service-account password as a write-only plaintext request field.
FSx for ONTAP SVM administrator passwords are supplied in write-only API fields.
FSx resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Global Accelerator tag values are plaintext metadata.
Glue connection properties can return plaintext usernames, passwords, URLs, and custom connector credentials when HidePassword is false.
Glue job argument maps are plaintext and commonly carry --password, --token, or connection values.
Glue ETL scripts in S3 can hard-code credentials and configuration files.
Workflow run properties are a mutable plaintext map shared between jobs and crawlers.
Data Catalog table and SerDe parameter maps can contain connection strings or custom storage credentials.
Schema Registry definitions can contain examples, defaults, field names, or literals revealing sensitive data.

sites.location: CloudWatch Logs Glue job/crawler log event.message
sites.description: ETL code and connector errors can echo arguments, records, and credentials into CloudWatch Logs.
Glue resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
GuardDuty findings contain access-key IDs, principal names, network endpoints, process/file details, Kubernetes identities, and sampled activity evidence.
Trusted IP set files can reveal private partners, scanner ranges, or sensitive network allowlists; the S3 object is the authoritative content.
Custom threat-intelligence files can expose confidential indicators and internal investigation data.
GuardDuty resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
IAM user tag values are customer-controlled plaintext and are readable by IAM APIs.
IAM role tag values can accidentally contain credentials or internal sensitive identifiers.
An inline IAM user policy can embed sensitive literals in condition keys or other customer-authored JSON.
An inline IAM role policy can embed sensitive literals in condition keys or other customer-authored JSON.
An inline IAM group policy can embed sensitive literals in condition keys or other customer-authored JSON.
A customer-managed policy version is URL-encoded JSON and can contain sensitive condition values.
The secret half of a new IAM access key is returned once in the creation response.
A CodeCommit/Keyspaces service-specific password is returned only when the credential is created or reset.
An administrator supplies an IAM user's console password in plaintext to the login-profile write API; it is never readable afterward.
An imported server certificate's PEM private key is supplied in plaintext to IAM and is not returned by read APIs.
Image Builder component documents contain shell/PowerShell commands, files, and parameters that can embed credentials.
Recipe-level user-data overrides are plaintext bootstrap scripts.
Component parameter values in recipes can be used to pass plaintext secrets into build steps.
Inline Dockerfile template data may hard-code build arguments, repository credentials, or secrets.
Image Builder workflow YAML can include command parameters and literals containing secrets.
Image Builder resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Inspector findings reveal vulnerable package paths, Lambda layers, repository/source locations, network reachability, instance metadata, and code-vulnerability context.
CIS scan reports expose host configuration, control failures, resource identifiers, and potentially sensitive operating-system details through a download URL.
Inspector resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Keyspaces rows are arbitrary application data and may contain plaintext credentials.
Keyspaces table tag values are plaintext metadata.
Kinesis stream records contain arbitrary producer data and may carry plaintext credentials or sensitive events.
Kinesis stream tag values are plaintext metadata.
KMS Decrypt returns the plaintext bytes of caller-supplied ciphertext when key policy and IAM permissions allow it.
GenerateDataKey deliberately returns a plaintext data-encryption key alongside its encrypted copy.
GenerateDataKeyPair returns a plaintext private key unless the WithoutPlaintext variant is used.
GenerateRandom returns raw random bytes that callers often adopt as passwords, keys, or signing secrets.

sites.location: CloudTrail event requestParameters.encryptionContext for KMS Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey
sites.description: KMS encryption context is not secret and is logged in plaintext to CloudTrail; applications must not put confidential values in it.
KMS key descriptions are free-form plaintext and should not contain confidential values.
KMS key tag values are plaintext metadata and are visible to principals with tag-read access.
Lake Formation work-unit results stream Apache Arrow rows from governed tables and may contain sensitive data.
Row-filter expressions are customer-authored strings and can contain sensitive literal values.
LF-Tag values are plaintext classification metadata and may disclose sensitive business or identity information.
Data lake settings parameters are customer-controlled string values.
Lambda environment variables are returned as plaintext to authorized readers even though Lambda encrypts them at rest.
Function deployment packages can contain hard-coded credentials, private keys, or sensitive configuration files.
Shared Lambda layer archives may include credentials or configuration that leaks into every consuming function.
Lambda function tag values are plaintext metadata.
Lightsail container deployments retain plaintext environment variable maps.
Container command arrays may expose credentials passed on the command line.
Lightsail exposes a managed database's master password through a dedicated read API.
Lightsail instance user data can contain bootstrap secrets; the API does not provide a corresponding post-create read field.
Lightsail instance tag values are returned in the instance description.
Lightsail container-service tag values are returned in service descriptions.
Macie can reveal up to ten actual sensitive-data occurrences per type from a finding; values are returned through the reveal workflow.
Macie findings disclose sensitive-data types, counts, exact file/record locations, bucket/object identifiers, and affected-resource metadata.
Custom data identifier regexes and word lists can accidentally include literal production secrets used as test patterns.
Allow-list regexes or word-list objects may contain real identifiers or secrets copied to suppress findings.
Macie resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
MemoryDB stores arbitrary Redis values, including sessions and plaintext credentials; data reads require network access and Redis/IAM authentication.
MemoryDB user passwords are supplied as write-only request fields.
MemoryDB resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Amazon MQ broker user passwords are write-only plaintext request fields.
ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ configuration XML is base64-encoded and can contain authentication, endpoint, or plugin configuration values.
Broker queues and topics carry arbitrary application payloads and headers; access is controlled by broker users and network policy rather than a message-read IAM API.

sites.location: CloudWatch Logs Amazon MQ general/audit log event.message
sites.description: Broker logs may expose usernames, client IDs, destinations, connection strings, and authentication failures.
Amazon MQ resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Kafka topics contain arbitrary message keys, values, and headers that may carry plaintext credentials.
MSK server.properties content is base64-encoded plaintext and custom properties may include sensitive endpoints or values.

sites.location: CloudWatch Logs/S3/Firehose MSK broker log record
sites.description: Broker logs can expose client principal names, topic names, connection errors, and occasionally authentication/configuration details.
MSK resource tag values are plaintext metadata.

sites.location: Neptune HTTPS Gremlin/SPARQL/openCypher query result body
sites.description: Graph vertices, edges, and properties are arbitrary customer data and may include credentials.
Neptune Streams can retain old and new graph changes, including rotated or deleted secret-bearing properties.
Neptune cluster parameter values are plaintext configuration strings.
Neptune resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Suricata rules are free-form plaintext and content matches may accidentally include real tokens, passwords, or confidential protocol values.
Rule variable definitions expose private network ranges and may contain misplaced sensitive strings.

sites.location: CloudWatch Logs/S3/Firehose Network Firewall log record

read.response_path: log event message or object body

sites.description: Firewall alert and flow records can reveal application metadata and, depending on rule/log content, fragments of packet data.
Network Firewall resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
OpenSearch indexes store arbitrary JSON documents and are commonly used for logs containing credentials or sensitive fields.
Serverless collection documents may contain plaintext credentials and sensitive application or log data.
SAML IdP metadata is stored plaintext and can reveal internal identity-provider endpoints, entity IDs, and signing certificates.
OpenSearch logs can contain query text, request paths, user identities, and application errors with document values.
OpenSearch resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
OpsWorks app environment variables are returned by DescribeApps, including values marked Secure.
Application source configuration may contain repository passwords or SSH private keys.
OpsWorks app SSL configuration can expose the PEM private key through DescribeApps.
Registered RDS connection records can expose the database password stored for app deployment.
Stack custom JSON is supplied to Chef recipes and is frequently used for configuration secrets.
Deployment command argument maps can contain plaintext credentials delivered to recipes.
OpsWorks resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
An AWS account's root email address is sensitive recovery and identity data visible through Organizations.
Customer-authored SCP, RCP, tag, backup, or AI-services policy JSON can accidentally contain sensitive literals.
Organization, OU, account, and policy tag values are plaintext customer metadata.
PartiQL query results can expose arbitrary ledger documents containing credentials or sensitive data.
A QLDB journal export contains the immutable history of every document, including deleted or rotated secrets, in S3.
QLDB ledger tag values are plaintext metadata.
QuickSight data-source credentials are supplied in write-only request fields; describe APIs do not return plaintext passwords.
Custom SQL definitions are stored plaintext and can contain literal credentials or sensitive business filters.

sites.location: DescribeAnalysisDefinition.Definition (filters, parameters, calculated fields, static values)
sites.description: Analysis definitions can retain sensitive parameter defaults, filter values, calculated-field literals, and annotations.
Dashboard definitions can expose static values, parameters, calculated fields, and business-sensitive labels.
A QuickSight embed URL contains a short-lived bearer token that creates the requested user session.
An anonymous QuickSight embed URL contains a short-lived bearer token authorizing the embedded session.
QuickSight resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
RAM resource-share and permission tag values are plaintext customer metadata.
A customer-managed RAM permission template is free-form policy JSON and may contain sensitive condition values.
RDS master passwords are plaintext write-only request fields and are never returned by DescribeDBInstances or DescribeDBClusters.
Aurora Data API query results may return arbitrary database rows containing credentials or sensitive data.
Database logs can contain SQL text, errors, connection details, and application-supplied values.
Engine parameter values are plaintext strings and extension parameters may be misused for sensitive configuration.
RDS resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
GetClusterCredentials returns a temporary database password for the selected database user.
Redshift cluster master passwords are supplied as write-only plaintext API inputs.
Redshift Data API result rows can contain arbitrary warehouse data and stored credentials.
Submitted SQL text can contain literal passwords, tokens, or sensitive filter values.
Cluster parameter values are plaintext and may include extension or logging configuration with sensitive literals.
Redshift resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Roles Anywhere CreateSession returns temporary role credentials to a certificate-authenticated caller and is not authorized by an IAM action on that caller.
A Roles Anywhere profile session policy is customer-authored JSON and can contain sensitive condition literals.
Trust-anchor and profile tag values are plaintext metadata.
TXT and other DNS record values can publish verification tokens, API keys, internal host data, or other secrets.
A health-check response search string is customer-controlled plaintext and may reproduce a sensitive response fragment.

sites.location: CloudWatch Logs Route 53 query log event.message
sites.description: DNS query logs reveal queried names; applications that place credentials or user identifiers in hostnames leak them into logs.
Hosted-zone and health-check tag values are plaintext metadata.
S3 object bodies are arbitrary customer content and are a primary location for plaintext credentials and sensitive datasets.
User-defined x-amz-meta-* object metadata is plaintext and may contain tokens or sensitive identifiers.
S3 object tag values are customer-controlled plaintext.
Bucket policy JSON can embed sensitive principals, identifiers, and condition literals in customer-authored statements.
S3 bucket tag values are plaintext metadata.
Website redirect targets and replacement keys are plaintext and can accidentally embed tokens or sensitive query-like values.
Notebook lifecycle scripts are base64-encoded shell scripts and commonly contain package tokens or bootstrap credentials.
Studio lifecycle scripts can hard-code credentials installed into every user or app environment.
Model container environment maps are plaintext configuration returned by DescribeModel.
Training environment and hyperparameter maps can contain plaintext credentials and proprietary configuration.
Processing-job environment variables are plaintext and may expose data-source credentials.
Batch-transform job environment variables are plaintext and may expose data-source credentials.
SageMaker pipeline JSON can hard-code parameters, environment variables, commands, and data locations containing credentials.

sites.location: Notebook Instance or Studio EFS home-directory files
sites.description: Notebook cells, outputs, shell history, .env files, and AWS credential files persist on notebook storage; there is no generic SageMaker file-content read API.

sites.location: CloudWatch Logs SageMaker training/processing/inference log event.message
sites.description: User containers can log environment variables, sample records, model inputs, and errors containing sensitive data.
SageMaker resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Secrets Manager deliberately stores arbitrary secret material and returns the selected version to authorized callers.
BatchGetSecretValue can return plaintext values for multiple secrets in one response.
A secret resource policy is customer-authored JSON and may itself contain sensitive condition values.
Secret descriptions are plaintext metadata and should not repeat the secret value.
Secret tag values are plaintext metadata even when the secret value is protected.
ASFF findings contain producer- and user-controlled notes, custom fields, resource details, and descriptions that can hold pasted credentials or sensitive evidence.
Custom finding producers can persist arbitrary sensitive text and maps in ASFF fields.
Automation-rule actions can write static note text and user-defined values into every matching finding.
Security Hub resource tag values are plaintext metadata.
Service Catalog exposes CloudFormation record outputs; products that output secrets make them readable here.
A provisioning artifact's CloudFormation template can hard-code credentials in parameters, metadata, mappings, properties, or outputs.
TagOption values are customer-controlled plaintext propagated to provisioned resources.
SNS accepts arbitrary message bodies and attributes; sensitive values are copied to subscriptions and cannot be read back from SNS itself.
